transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess my wife thought it might be good for me to talk to someone, though I’m not sure it’s really a “me” problem exactly. It’s just… for about a year now, these things at her work—late meetings, little changes in the messages she sends, the timing of things—they line up too neatly to just be normal office stuff.

She says it’s nothing, and I know offices can be chaotic, I worked in a department where meetings got moved constantly, especially around finals, but this feels different. Like there’s a kind of private signal in it, something she’s trying to tell me without actually saying it. I suppose that’s why I’m here.
Have you ever heard voices, sounds, or seen things that other people around you didn't seem to notice or couldn't hear or see?

No, I don’t think so. I mean, not like hearing a voice in the room or seeing someone who isn’t there. Sometimes I’ll notice things other people brush off, like timing or patterns, but that’s not the same as a sound or a vision. 

I’ve always been pretty observant, honestly—when you work around students you get used to reading between the lines—but no, I wouldn’t say I’m hearing or seeing things others can’t.

Over this past year, have you also noticed times when your mood was unusually high, energetic, or irritable—or alternatively, periods of deep sadness or loss of interest in things—that lasted for days or weeks?

I don’t know that I’d put it that way. I mean, everyone has good days and bad days, right? Especially when you’re paying attention to something and trying to make sense of it.

I wouldn’t say I’ve been, you know, wildly energetic or anything like that. Irritable, maybe sometimes, but my wife would probably say that’s because I keep circling back to the same concerns. And sadness… I don’t know. I still do my usual things. Work has its own rhythm, and teaching assistants kind of get pulled into whatever crisis students are having that week, so it’s hard to separate mood from just being worn out.

So… no, not really days or weeks of some big mood change that I’ve noticed.
Aside from these concerns about your wife, has your ability to function at work or in your daily routine changed at all over this past year?

No, not in the main things. I mean, I’m still showing up for my teaching sections, and I keep up with the data analysis. That part has a structure to it, which helps—students come in with the same kinds of questions every semester, honestly, even when they think they’re the first ones to ask.

And I still ride my bike, meet a couple friends for chess when we can. So day-to-day, I wouldn’t say I’ve fallen apart or anything.

The trouble is mostly at home, with my wife. We get stuck in these arguments about what her schedule really means, and then the whole evening can get swallowed by it. That’s where it causes problems, more than work.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a持续 (~1 year) fixed, non-bizarre delusion of jealousy/infidelity involving his wife, interpreting neutral events (meeting timing, message wording) as coded signals of an affair. He denies hallucinations, thought disorder, or other psychotic symptoms, and explicitly denies manic or depressive mood episodes lasting days to weeks. Functioning is well preserved in occupational and social domains (teaching, data analysis, cycling, chess with friends), with impairment confined specifically to the marital relationship, which is consistent with encapsulated delusional disorder rather than schizophrenia (no hallucinations/disorganization) or a mood disorder with psychotic features (no mood episode). This pattern—circumscribed, non-bizarre delusion, preserved functioning outside the delusion's theme, duration >1 month—fits Delusional Disorder (F22), jealous subtype.
